sections.h2: What routes lead to a sale of a Lancaster, NY house?
sections.html:
Three routes lead to a sale in Lancaster: an agent listing, a sale between you and a buyer you find yourself, and a direct cash purchase. Which one fits depends on how soon you need to be done and what shape the building is in. A tidy ranch with no deadline suits a listing. A house with a failing roof, a probate to settle or a tenant who will not leave tends to suit a quick, as-is buyer.

  • Agent listing: wide exposure, with showings, a lender's appraisal and the chance a buyer's financing falls through.
  • Owner-handled sale: you set price and terms, and your attorney drafts the contract and deed.
  • Cash purchase: no repair requests and no mortgage contingency, since the buyer takes the property in its present state.

Every route ends the same way in Lancaster: a notarized deed, transfer tax forms for the Erie County Clerk, and settlement of whatever tax is still owed on the parcel.

sections.h2: Where is Lancaster, and what is it like for homeowners?
sections.html:
Lancaster sits in Erie County, roughly 11 miles east of downtown Buffalo, on about 37 square miles with two villages inside its borders, Lancaster and Depew. According to the town's history page, it was carved out of Clarence by the State Legislature in 1833, the Village of Lancaster incorporated in 1849, and Depew followed in 1894. Five major railroads once crossed the town, and the rail lines are still active.

Residents numbered 45,075 in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, nearly identical to the 45,106 counted in 2020. The Town tax office says five school districts bill Lancaster addresses: Lancaster Central, Depew Union Free, Alden Central, Clarence Central and Iroquois Central. Most of the town falls in Lancaster Central, yet the district printed on your tax bill is the one to quote to buyers.

Getting around is easy by car. The Thruway (I-90) crosses the north end, NY 33 runs just below it, US 20 follows Broadway through the middle, and NY 78 (Transit Road) forms the western edge. East of Bowen Road the town is still filling in and keeps a more rural feel.

Heritage counts for something in the village. Twelve Lancaster buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places, eleven of them along Broadway in the Village of Lancaster Historic District and one, the Hull House on Genesee Street, in the town. The Building Department's page carries a Village of Lancaster historic preservation application, so owners near Broadway should ask the village what review applies before promising a buyer a facade or window project.

sections.h2: How do Lancaster home values and household figures compare?
sections.html:
The middle owner-occupied home in Lancaster is valued at $277,600, with about four in five homes lived in by their owners. That gives you a rough anchor, though a survey median cannot price an individual house, so ask for recent nearby sales before you settle on a number. The profile below draws on the Census Bureau's Lancaster town profile.

sections.h2: Will the Lancaster Building Department care about my past renovations?
sections.html:
It can, because the Building Department enforces the state building and fire code, zoning, stormwater practices and flood plain rules across both the town and the village. The department's page says that nobody may build, alter, move or demolish a structure without first obtaining a permit.

Applications are posted for decks, fences, pools and hot tubs, sheds, signs, demolition and one- and two-family dwellings, along with a handout on as-built survey requirements. If a deck, an addition or a finished basement was added before you bought, ask the office whether the project is on file and was signed off. A clear answer saves negotiating time later.

  • Inspections tied to a permit are booked by phone with the office, which keeps weekday hours.
  • The department also links resources on vacant and "zombie" properties, handy for an inherited house that has sat empty.
  • Truck routes and yard sale permits are separate matters handled through the town and its Highway Department.

sections.h2: What are the Lancaster tax deadlines, and what happens to late payments?
sections.html:
Town and County bills are due February 15 and school bills October 15, pushed back a day if the date lands on a weekend or holiday. The Town's tax office, which sits inside the Town Clerk's office, collects both. A mailed check is on time only when the postmark carries the due date or an earlier one, and the office states there are no exceptions.

School tax picks up a 7.5% penalty for the rest of October and 9% through November. Whatever is unpaid after November 30 goes onto the Erie County tax roll. Town and County penalties begin at 1.5% in the first two weeks late and reach 7.5% by the end of April, and interest runs after that.

The town office takes Town and County payments through June 30 and school payments through November 30. Past those dates, payments and payoff questions go to Erie County Real Property Tax Services in Buffalo. Interest changes the payoff monthly, so request a county figure before fixing a closing date.

sections.h2: What will the Erie County Clerk charge on a Lancaster deed?
sections.html:
Erie County adds its own transfer tax to the state's, for a combined $4.50 per $500 of price, split $2.00 state and $2.50 county, and the seller is responsible for it. The Clerk's deed page rounds the price up to the next $500, so a sale at Lancaster's $277,600 median value would owe about $2,502.

Recording adds a $45 statutory fee, $5 for each page, $10 to file the TP-584 and $125 to file the RP-5217 report for residential property. The deed itself must carry original signatures, a notary's acknowledgment, a full legal description and street addresses for every party, since P.O. boxes are rejected.

  • An owner aged 62 or older who has lived in a one- or two-family house for a year or more can claim the reduced $2.00-per-$500 rate.
  • Residential sales at $1 million or above add a 1% mansion tax that the buyer pays.
  • The Clerk also asks for a Notice of Sale or Transfer of Ownership on residential property.

State guidance on the Tax Department's transfer tax page sets the TP-584 and payment at 15 days after delivery of the deed. Afterward, close out your STAR registration through the state's STAR page, and let the new owner register for the credit.

faqs.q: Which office collects tax on a Lancaster property?
faqs.a: The Lancaster tax office, part of the Town Clerk's office, collects Town, County and school bills. Later payments, after June 30 for Town and County or November 30 for school, go to Erie County Real Property Tax Services in Buffalo.

faqs.q: Does Lancaster belong to one school district?
faqs.a: No. Lancaster Central covers most of it, yet Depew Union Free, Alden Central, Clarence Central and Iroquois Central also bill Lancaster addresses, per the Town tax office. Read your own tax bill to see which one applies.

faqs.q: Who covers transfer tax on a Lancaster sale?
faqs.a: The seller covers the state and Erie County transfer tax when the deed reaches the County Clerk. The total is $4.50 per $500, and qualifying owners aged 62 and over may pay a reduced $2.00 rate.

faqs.q: Must I get a permit before listing my Lancaster house?
faqs.a: A plain sale does not appear among the permit triggers. The Building Department's rule covers building, altering, moving and demolishing, so use a call to the office to confirm that earlier decks, pools or additions were permitted and closed out.

faqs.q: Is a damaged Lancaster house still sellable?
faqs.a: Yes. You can market it as-is to investors, list it and price in the repairs, or take cash from a buyer who purchases without a repair list. Check with the Building Department about open permits before accepting any offer.
